utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-95-10/1-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We are here today for a Status Conference in the case of the Prosecution against you, Mr. Cesic, but before continuing, I'll ask you whether you can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Cesic. As we discussed before, sometimes it's easier, as far as the microphone is concerned, that you remain seated, because you have to bend over again and again to make yourself heard, and therefore I wouldn't mind if I address you or if you give an answer, that you remain seated. But as you wish. Yes. Please be seated, then. May I have the appearances for the Prosecution first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Mark Harmon. Appearing with me today, Mr. Vladimir Tochilovsky and Mr. Thomas Hannis and case manager Susan Grogan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac and I represent the accused Ranko Cesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, I think it's for the first time that we meet in this formal setting, because at the last Status Conference Mr. Cesic was still represented by another counsel. Welcome. I suggest to you that we would deal with the matters the same matters as have been discussed yesterday during the 65 ter meeting, and Mr. Cesic, since you were not there, I'll just briefly inform you, you might have been informed already, but I'll just briefly inform you that the major issues discussed at this agenda were the disclosure, that is, information from one party to another, how many witnesses the Prosecution intended to present at trial, and whether there was any need for protective measures, whether there was any agreement on matters of fact between the parties. The pre-trial work plan was discussed. The preparation for today's Status Conference was discussed, and some other matters which I'll not go into in any detail at this very moment. Would there be anything to be added to that on the agenda? I read the transcript of the 65 ter meeting and I noticed that specifically the potential application of Rule 11 bis would need further attention. So we'll pay specific attention to that at a later stage. But apart from that, is there any other issue you'd like to raise? If you'd prefer to add something to the agenda in closed session or if you'd like to say something in closed session, please apply for it. But is there any addition to the agenda requested?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's nothing on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is nothing that the Defence would like to add, nothing in addition to the issues that we discussed at the 65 ter meeting yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Then the first issue discussed yesterday was disclosure, and as far as I understood, the parties have no specific requests as far as disclosure is concerned. I do understand that the Defence might not have concentrated mainly on that during the past period, but there's nothing specifically to deal with in respect of disclosure. Is that correct, Mr. Bakrac? Yes. I see you're nodding for the transcript, nodding yes. I take it that the Prosecution takes the same position, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We expressed our position yesterday in complete detail. We have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So no problems in that respect. Then the next issue would be the number of witnesses the Prosecution would like to present. As I read from the transcript of yesterday, that the Prosecution has in mind to present 14 live witnesses at trial and two experts under Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are still juggling with the figures in terms of the 92 bis witnesses. We expect to present at least two witnesses, 92 bis, and possibly a third witness 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did I well understand that at least the two you have in mind were expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is what we said yesterday. We have two witnesses -- two expert witnesses who would be 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for my better understanding, Mr. Harmon: As we all know, Rule 94 bis deals with testimony of expert witnesses. Is it because of the testimony earlier given in other cases that you'd rather rely on 92 bis where you could include also parts of the transcripts --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. These experts testified in the Jelisic case. On that basis we would submit their testimonies and their expert statements. I suggest that that written evidence be accepted by the Court in lieu of oral testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes and rule 94 bis would only provide for the acceptance of an expert statement and not for testimony -- transcript of testimony given in other cases. That's the reason why you rely on 92 bis rather than 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least clear to me what determines your preference for 92 bis. So I do understand you're still considering a third expert. I don't hope that after every night's sleep another witness will be added in your mind, but as far as the agreement on facts is concerned, I do understand that Defence could expect a proposal from the Prosecution, and, well, not having received it, Mr. Bakrac, of course, you could not take any position in respect of that but I take it you'll then consider what the -- yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in terms of adjudicated facts since the previous case that was litigated ended with a plea of guilty there could be no adjudicated facts as I understand the current jurisprudence in this institution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It should be adjudicated as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Consequently, an agreement on the facts would rely on an agreement of those facts which are expressed within the indictment itself which would entail counsel and I getting together and going through the indictment and seeing if there are any facts that would be the subject of an agreement. Those are the facts I'm talking about in terms of any agreements in fact and not adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. And I also now understand that you might not come up with a proposal ready to accept or not to accept but rather to sit together, and since I, with great joy, read that both parties seem to appreciate the relationship as professional and constructive, we'll hear what the outcome of that communication will be. Then going to the next point of the agenda, I do understand that the investigation as far as the Prosecution is concerned is completed, that the Prosecution would be ready at relatively short notice to file a pre-trial brief, and of course with all the annexes to be added to that. And as far as I understand, Mr. Bakrac, the Defence has not fully completed its investigations, but is at a level of preparation which would allow to join in the schedule as it has been suggested yesterday. I'll come to that soon. The schedule suggested would include that mid-September the Office of the Prosecution could file a pre-trial brief, that the Defence could do so after some three weeks, that means by the 10th of October; that a Pre-Trial Conference would be feasible for the end of October, and that then the case would be ready to be heard by a Trial Chamber. This brings me to the next point and perhaps one of the issues that has created some confusion, and that is the potential application of Rule 11 bis, referral of the case. I do understand that the confusion is not limited to you, Mr. Bakrac, but also to Mr. Cesic. So therefore, since it has been a very short time since yesterday, I will try briefly to explain first what the view of myself, as Pre-Trial Judge, on the issue is, and also in respect of the time schedules involved. Mr. Cesic, Rule 11 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence provide for a possibility that the Tribunal refers a case to the authorities of another state, and that would then be the state on whose territory the crime has been committed or in which you the accused - that would be you - would be arrested. The state where the events, the acts with which you are charged were committed is the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'd like, for practical reasons, to concentrate on that. What would that mean, a referral of the case? That would mean that the president of the Tribunal appoints a Trial Chamber to consider whether a specific case should be referred to such a state. The President can do that just by its own, on its own initiative, but it could also be the initiative of the Prosecution asking the President to assign the Trial Chamber. Before a referral will take place, you will be heard, since you're in The Hague, that would be different if you would be at large, but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you would then be heard. The Rules also indicate what kind of cases would qualify for such a referral. The indication refers to a Security Council presidential statement in which it says that the gravity of the crimes charged and the level of responsibility of the accused should be taken into consideration. If we look at your case, then the gravity of the crimes charged could not be qualified as the most serious of cases of the Tribunal, without ignoring the consequences for victims. And I'm not expressing myself on who is responsible for those crimes - but the crimes as they are charged - without ignoring the importance for those who were as victims involved in those crimes. The crimes you're charged with are, although serious, are compared to other cases relatively limited, especially in number. Of the a little bit over ten counts, most of your acts have been described in two different legal ways. We find some six people who died according to the charges, and we have a case of sexual assault on two charges. Compared to other cases, and I emphasise compared to other cases, they are of less importance for this Tribunal. This Tribunal is mainly established to hear the most serious crimes. The same is true for the level of responsibility. There are other accused who have to appear before this Tribunal who had a higher level of responsibility according to their military or police or civilian rank. Therefore, your case, looking at this criteria, might well qualify for a referral. What would that mean? That would mean that you would send back and all the information would be sent back as well, and if I say sent back, that presumably would be to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in order to avoid any misunderstanding, most likely to Sarajevo, because during a certain period of time now preparations are ongoing for the establishment of a special court in Sarajevo which would hear such cases. The Prosecutor might send observers to proceedings that would take place as a consequence of such a referral, and the Rules do not fully exclude a possibility of the case taken back to the Tribunal, although you'll understand that that's not the purpose of a referral, so that, I would say, would be under exceptional circumstances. I explained to you this referral in order to be satisfied that you are perfectly aware of what a referral means. If you would have any questions in this respect, things that might not be clear to you, please ask them, so that no confusion remains. Part of the confusion seems to be the result of, at the one hand, the scheduling in time for the preparation of a trial before this Tribunal; and at the same time, alluding to the possibility of a referral of this case to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Cases in this Tribunal are heard by a Trial Chamber whenever they are ready to be heard - that means that the parties have completed the preparation for trial - and when a Trial Chamber is available to hear that case. What we discussed a couple of minutes ago was how the parties would complete their preparation for trial, and as you may have noticed, it appears that the parties would be ready for trial in two and a half months approximately from now on in -- I have to check what I exactly said, but I think it was in October. No, it was November. So by the beginning of November, the parties would be ready for trial. The second condition was that there's a Trial Chamber available to hear your case. The Trial Chambers are, if I could say it this way, are fully booked at this moment. Nevertheless, sometimes cases which were expected to take a couple of months might be finished earlier, other cases might take more time than we could expect. Your case is a relatively small case. You have been in the Tribunal in detention in The Hague since a little bit over one year. Well, it's not a surprise to you that you're not the detainee who is longest in detention at this moment, so for that reason you might not be one of the first cases that could be heard. Therefore, what we know at this moment, that the parties will be ready for trial by the beginning of November. Whether the case will be heard next year March, next year August, or next year December, we do not know. That is a matter of priority, in which many considerations will be -- where many circumstances will be considered, such as length of pre-trial detention, kind of case, time the case will take. So therefore, it's very difficult to predict when it will be your turn when your case will be heard by a Trial Chamber. The preparations for a special court in Sarajevo are such that we could expect that in the second half of next year, cases might be referred to such a court. If your case has not been heard by then in the Tribunal, it might well be that your case will then be referred, at least the case as such would qualify for it. So therefore, as far as there was any confusion, you have to understand that preparation for trial is completed so that your case could be heard whenever a Trial Chamber is available. And if a Trial Chamber is available, keeping in mind the priorities set by the Tribunal, then your case will be heard. If your case has not yet been heard and if there is -- if the conditions for referral are met, your case might be referred. That is, in general, the situation you could expect. If you would have -- or if your counsel or if the Prosecution would have any questions in this respect, I would like to hear those questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have no questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No Your Honour, the Defence doesn't have any questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cesic, it's your case so therefore I specifically ask you whether you have any questions in this respect and whether the confusion that might have existed, if there was any confusion, has been clarified by this explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your detailed explanation. Everything is clear to me. I have been informed by my counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should have relied more on you being informed by counsel. On the other hand, I was aware that that might be a risk also on the basis of what has been said yesterday during the 65 ter meeting that there might be some confusion. So therefore I preferred to explain it to you myself, so that there would be a direct explanation and no risk of miscommunication. Having explained this and looking at my agenda, I see that the next 65 ter meeting has been scheduled for the 1st of September, 2003. Are there any other matters on the agenda? I have at least one issue, Mr. Cesic. At previous occasion you have told me that you have no health problems. I hope that it's still the same. If not, please tell me, and if there would be any other specific problems in respect of your detention situation or whatever other problem, please tell me. And if you'd prefer to do that in closed session because of the privacy involved, you can apply for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is no need to go into private session. Everything is all right. I'm in good health, and the conditions are good. Everything is in good order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cesic. Is there anything one of the parties would like to raise? Mr. Bakrac, is there anything you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you very much. I believe that at yesterday's 65 ter conference, we were very constructive, and everything that could have become an issue, and everything pertaining to the way we are to proceed, has been thoroughly discussed, so that I have no further issues to raise and no questions, especially in view of the fact that you are also fully informed of everything that took place at yesterday's 65 ter conference. So there is no need to repeat anything. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there are no further issues on behalf of the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then I think we have dealt with all the issues that were on the agenda and we'll adjourn this hearing.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
